Hayden Panettiere’s claims that Neutrogena ended their 10-year partnership after she spoke out about postpartum depression are going viral following the actor’s tragic death on Sunday.

In her 2026 memoir ‘This Is Me: A Reckoning’ and interviews during her press tour in May, Panettiere alleged the company fired her for violating a contractual “morals clause” after she opened up about her postpartum experience on ‘Live with Kelly and Michael’ in 2015.

At the time, she called her postpartum struggles “really painful… really scary, and women need a lot of support,” adding, “there’s a lot of misunderstanding, and I feel like there’s a lot of people out there who think that it’s not real.”

In a viral clip from Jay Shetty’s ‘On Purpose’ podcast posted in May, she said being dropped was the last thing she expected, adding that she never planned to discuss postpartum depression on the show, but she “wouldn’t change it for the world.” 

Now, Neutrogena’s social media is flooded with people slamming the brand and calling for a boycott. Swipe through for some of the discourse. 

RIP Hayden 🤍

Hayden Panettiere, 36, reportedly passed away Sunday, just five days before her 37th birthday.

“She was an incredible light and a force of nature who brought immeasurable love and joy to all who knew her - and to the millions who watched her onscreen,” her father said in a statement.

Panettiere’s career catapulted with a breakout performance in ‘Remember the Titans,’ followed by iconic roles in film and television, including ‘Heroes,’ the ‘Scream’ franchise, ‘Nashville,’ and more.

In May, the actor released her tell-all memoir, ‘This Is Me: A Reckoning,’ chronicling her life and struggles with depression and addiction following years of abuse in Hollywood.

Clips from her final interview on the ‘On Purpose with Jay Shetty’ podcast are trending. During the conversation, Panettiere opened up about some of the abuse she endured, including a casting she attended at 18 on a boat, where she said she was forced onto a bed with a “famous” naked man. 

She also recalled learning that she had been dropped as the face of Neutrogena after ten years, allegedly because she spoke out about her postpartum depression. That revelation is now sparking calls on social media to boycott the company.

Panettiere also expressed that she was looking forward to a future after “shaking off all of this darkness” and hoped she “had a lot more life to live.” 💔

RIP Hayden 🕊️

Edible-inspired scents known as gourmand fragrances have taken over #PerfumeTok, fueling a viral comeback for @yslbeauty’s 2014 eau de parfum, Black Opium, based on the 1977 classic. Building on that buzz and a growing appetite for gourmand, YSL Beauty introduces Black Opium Pink Glaze, which puts a spin on the original’s signature coffee-forward scent with playful notes like “juicy strawberry” and “sensual jasmine.”

The brand has tapped Alisha Boe as its new Global Ambassador for Black Opium, a refreshingly unexpected pick for one of luxury’s biggest fragrance franchises. The Gen Z actor (‘The Buccaneers,’ ‘13 Reasons Why’) embodies what YSL Beauty calls “the new BLACK OPIUM woman: magnetic, confident, main character energy.” In an AP interview about the campaign, Boe called the moment “very surreal” and joked that she hopes “all her exes” see the billboards.

Gourmand is a relatively young fragrance category, often traced back to Mugler’s groundbreaking 1992 release Angel, whose dessert-inspired scent profile transformed what luxury perfume could smell like. More than three decades later, gourmand has become one of fragrance’s biggest categories.

Gen Z and Millennial shoppers are driving the momentum, with gourmands accounting for about 55 percent of new purchase intentions in younger demographics and nearly 42 percent of overall fragrance preferences, according to a Reanin report. Future Market Insights projects the gourmand market will grow from $32.5B in 2025 to $55B by 2035. Fragrance lovers are craving scents that smell good enough to eat and YSL Beauty is ready to serve.

Black Opium Pink Glaze drops on YSLBeautyUS.com and at Ulta on Aug. 23, with a nationwide release on Sept. 22.

Do you have big feelings about John Galliano?

When the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced John Galliano as the subject of next year’s Costume Institute exhibition, and by extension the Met Gala, the response was unusually complicated for the fashion press. Alongside acknowledgments of Galliano’s influence came reminders of the antisemitic tirades that ended his tenure at Dior in 2011, raising a familiar question: can fashion celebrate the work without rehabilitating the person?

That tension has followed Galliano through his return. After apologizing, undergoing treatment, and spending years largely outside fashion, he resurfaced at Maison Margiela in 2014. Over the next decade, he rebuilt his reputation through the clothes, culminating in an acclaimed 2024 Artisanal collection. But if that marked Galliano’s return, what’s happening now looks more like canonization.

Between the Met retrospective and his new relationship with Zara, which has produced custom looks for Stevie Nicks and Bad Bunny, Galliano is being reintroduced through two of fashion’s biggest institutions. His influence is difficult to dispute; so is the history that made him a pariah. Centering him puts both on display.

But when controversy reliably generates clicks, are institutions merely accepting the controversy that comes with Galliano, or counting on it? Accountability doesn’t require erasing someone’s work, but acknowledging it doesn’t require sanding down the parts that make its celebration uncomfortable.

The Met has navigated controversial legacies before. Its 2023 Karl Lagerfeld retrospective came four years after his death, when his influence could be examined alongside his inflammatory comments without functioning as a comeback vehicle. Galliano presents a different proposition: he’s alive, working, designing for Zara, and once again at fashion’s center.

A retrospective is ostensibly about looking backward, but Galliano’s arrives as his next chapter is being written, and inevitably helps write it. So is revisiting Galliano’s past an inability to let him move beyond it, or exactly what accountability looks like when an industry decides someone deserves another turn at the center?

#FXPartner • Set in 1981, @TheShardsFX captures a moment when the style of the ‘70s lingered as the defining look of the ‘80s began to emerge. “[Ryan Murphy] really wanted to lean on 1979 into the early ‘80s and not do what everybody thinks of as typical eighties,” costume producer and co-executive producer Lou Eyrich said. With the launch of MTV alongside era-defining albums and films, 1981 served as both a stylistic and cultural crossroads that informed the costume department.

Rather than defining each character through an era-specific cliché or brand, costume designer Joshua Marsh explained that the team focused on “iconography and archetypes and thinking about these being the most elevated version of the tropes for each character.” Each character’s wardrobe became a visual representation of their interests and personality, and though they all possess distinct qualities, the throughline is prep.

Preppy style predates 1981; however, its visual language was solidified the year prior with the publication of The Official Preppy Handbook. Though the book was originally intended as a satirical jab at a niche subculture, as Marsh notes, “it became culture itself.” Marsh continues, “It can look incredible on so many different kinds of individuals, and it can always elevate so many different body types and personalities to this kind of classic, iconic look.” Alongside Ralph Lauren, The Official Preppy Handbook became a key reference point for the costume department, while the aesthetic helped establish the sense of maturity that radiates from these teenagers.

For these characters, dressing preppy became another way to perform adulthood. As Marsh explains, “I think one of the reasons that they feel so adult is that they are essentially living as adults. They’re these wealthy kids at this prep school in LA, but there’s no parents around ever…they’re just living free.”

Elon Musk’s company xAI has sued the state of Minnesota in federal court over a new law banning AI “nudification” technology, just days before it is set to take effect on Saturday. The lawsuit argues that the measure, signed by Gov. Tim Walz, violates the First Amendment by restricting “free speech” and “tools of visual expression.”

While federal and state laws already prohibit creating or distributing nonconsensual explicit AI deepfakes, Minnesota’s law is the first to hold AI companies responsible rather than only individual users, with a hefty fine of $500,000 per violation.

The lawsuit comes as xAI faces growing backlash over Grok, its chatbot available on X. Grok offers a “Spicy Mode” setting that can generate explicit content from user-uploaded images. 

State Rep. Jessica Hanson alleged that Grok is “the number one tool used to make child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” citing reports she says show a 26,000% increase in CSAM linked to the feature.

State Sen. Erin Maye Quade said she was “surprised” Musk’s attorneys found time to sue, arguing that xAI has already been sued multiple times over conduct the “exact conduct that is now illegal in the state of Minnesota.” 

Quade pointed to several pending lawsuits, including one brought by a U.K. lawmaker seeking to stop Grok after an AI-generated video depicted her “being prepared to be sexually assaulted.” She also referenced a lawsuit filed by an Arkansas family alleging Grok was used to create CSAM of their child, and a lawsuit in Tennessee brought by five minors who allege the technology was used to create CSAM of themselves.

But sure, leave it to a MAGAt to protect families, right?

In a viral joint statement shared Wednesday, BTS announced they won’t be submitting their hit comeback album ‘Arirang’ for 2027 Grammys consideration. The announcement comes just weeks after the Recording Academy unveiled a new Best Asian Pop Music category, which immediately raised eyebrows online. 

“We hope music itself can be heard and loved rather than being distinguished by region or language,” the K-pop group posted online in Korean. “We thank Army and everyone who has always stood by us.”

The Grammys add new categories every few years, but lately some additions are looking extra sus. After Beyoncé made history by winning both AOTY and Best Country Album for ‘Cowboy Carter,’ the Academy suddenly split its country categories into Contemporary and Traditional. Interesting timing 🤔 

Earlier this year, Bad Bunny’s ‘Debí Tirar Más Fotos’ became the first Spanish-language album to win AOTY and suddenly the Recording Academy is rolling out a Best Latin Song category for 2027…

BTS has performed at the Grammys three times, with “Butter” becoming the most-watched Grammy performance ever on YouTube. The group has also earned five Grammy nominations and still has yet to win any.

Although BTS would’ve been a major contender to win the first Best Asian Pop Music award, they’re making a statement by choosing to opt out entirely. And if anyone’s taking the L here, it’s probably the Grammys, who just lost their biggest engagement magnet before the category even debuted. Too bad.

Anyway... congrats to BTS on the sold-out world tour!

Trump mentioned Dylan Mulvaney not once, not twice, but four times during his White House Correspondents’ Dinner Speech on Friday, which was rescheduled after a gunman purportedly opened fire on the event in April.

The eyeroll-inducing statement happened while he singled out CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, who was in attendance to accept an award for her coverage of the White House. “She’s a young, attractive woman. She never smiles,” the president stated. Trump has repeatedly criticized Collins for “not smiling” during his second term.

He then compared Collins to Mulvaney in an attempt to make a joke. “I thought Kaitlan had really made it big with a major new sponsorship, but then I informed her that it wasn’t her on the Bud Light can, it was Dylan Mulvaney,” Trump said, referencing Mulvaney’s three-year-old ad campaign. On Sunday, Trump doubled down on Truth Social, posting an AI-generated image of Collins’ face on Mulvaney’s body.

Mulvaney, meanwhile, seemed largely unbothered. She said she was “incredibly honored” to be compared to Collins before dragging the president.

“It seems to me that I might be the one that got away for these men, like I am permanently burned into their retinas, I am microchipped into their minds,” she said. “Being publicly mocked and criticized by this administration is actually, like, the greatest compliment of all.”

She then questioned why she seems to live rent-free in MAGA’s minds. “Why is it so important to them that I don’t find success?... Oh my God... freedom! I am free in a way that they will never have the privilege to experience, and they want to use their power to take away my freedom.” she said.

“But what they don’t understand is my freedom has zero contingency on what they can provide for me, because my freedom is fully dependent on the moment that I acknowledged my real, authentic self.”

Mulvaney ended by urging viewers to support trans and nonbinary people, closing with a pointed message for Trump: “To the president, thank you for reminding me that I am more powerful than I even knew.”

Ever flipped through the glossy pages of Vogue and briefly wondered if you’d accidentally picked up National Geographic? Not even a year old, and Vogue India already had people talking. People like The New York Times.

The August 2008 issue returned to one of fashion’s favourite forms of pornography: poverty. The shoot wasn’t the usual luxury-editorial impulse of putting a model in couture next to a crumbling wall in the name of “juxtaposition.” These were actual, unnamed people living in what the NYT described as “in-your-face poverty.” They were photographed by Jean-François Campos (the shoot used to be available on his website, not anymore IJBOL) on the busy streets alongside objects of almost comical luxury: a Burberry umbrella, a Fendi baby bib, a Birkin. You know, the essentials.

The idea was to democratise fashion, to suggest that beautiful objects and the fantasy of luxury needn’t belong exclusively to the people who could afford them. But when the prices of the handbags featured were more than what the “real” people could earn in a lifetime, well, one must ring the alarm on the moral fashion faux pas.

Tasteless? Tasteful? Tone-deaf? Perhaps all three, which is partly why we’re still talking about it. But you have to admit that there was certainly an editorial appetite then. That compulsion to provoke, delight, shock, whatever, but above all to remain memorable. Asked for her two cents amid the controversy, then EIC Priya Tanna said to let them eat cake and “Lighten up.”

Before ‘Naagin’ held every television screen captive, Nagraj was our venomous obsession. Introduced in 1986 by Raj Comics, he was a cast-away-prince-turned-killing-machine-turned-hero in tight purple briefs and knee high boots. With power like Vishfunkaar (venom breath that can melt metal) and command over a million snakes that resided in him (character development before AI 🤣), he was THE most powerful hero in desi comic history.

What Raj Comics did was turn Indian mythology and stories into a format that the youth were already consuming ferociously from foreign publications. They changed Western settings and brought in local perspectives. Like why should super-villains only attack America? 🙂‍↕️ The success was immense, with every kid saving up to buy the latest issue (they were not CHEAP!) or rushing to the nearest stores to rent them out. 

With readership declining, Nagraj has been largely forgotten. No major Bollywood adaptation has been made (although Ranveer was rumoured to take on the role?) and it unfortunately seems to not be anywhere in sight. But for the millennials and the 90s kids, the memories are still vibrant as the coloured pages of those comic strips.

In 2011, pre-influ, pre-Instagram and pre-Reels flattening everyone into the same-same algo-approved person, Burberry brought Art of the Trench to India. The premise was deceptively simple and actually rather brilliant: take one evergreen object, the classic Burberry trench, and document how personal style mutates across cultures, cities and people. High and low, dressed up, dressed down, skinny jeans, ballet flats, etc. The India chapter was photographed by @man0u, who left the relative sanity of his nine-to-five job and has spent nearly two decades travelling all over India documenting street style via @wearaboutblog, in collaboration with editor @dalchodha, who curated and styled not only India but several Art of the Trench projects globally. Looking at the pictures now feels almost anthropological. The poses, henny! The skinny jeans? The ballet flats lol! An ankle-length jean with a ballet flat was basically formalwear. People seemingly wearing clothes because they liked them rather than because 14 other people had received the same PR mailer that morning. With all the humdrum about craft revival and preservation, another designer brings another craft to the runway. Anamika teamed up with a group of women artists who practice the age-old tradition of Kalighat paintings and had them meticulously hand-paint her couture garments. The paintings, on organza and silk satin, became a part of voluminous ball gowns, sherwanis, and sheer slip dresses. As awe-inspiring as it all may be, after the show, Anamika shares with us one bitter truth about craft and artisans—they are not making any money. Even with all the social media optics and engagement farming, most artisans are still not making any money. 

The Kalighat paintings are iconic and lend a huge visual identity to Kolkata, yet the lack of patronage confused Anamika. “Craft is not something to be wrapped in muslin, framed, and put on the walls. It needs to be current and relevant. It needs to be in people’s lives.”, she said. For her, craft is not stagnant and needs experimentation. She believes in preservation but not freezing it in a bygone era. 

We asked her if there is a right way of using craft, and even she says there may never be a definite answer but to continue to engage. “As long as we engage with it, that’s the only way to survive.”

Dion Lee deserved a different ending.

for 15 years, Dion Lee built one of those rare fashion languages you could recognise without ever seeing the label: technical construction, corsetry, cut-outs, hardware and clothes that somehow felt futuristic, architectural and extremely sexy all at once.

founded in Sydney in 2009, the brand went from Australian Fashion Week to New York, dressing everyone from Rosalía to Zendaya and Taylor Swift and becoming one of Australia’s biggest global fashion exports.

then, almost unbelievably, it unravelled. after long-time investor Cue withdrew its backing, the Australian business entered voluntary administration in May 2024 with liabilities later estimated at more than AUD $35 million. no acceptable buyer was found, and by August the companies behind the label were voted into liquidation.

a very abrupt ending for a brand that had such a ridiculously strong point of view.

we miss Dion Lee. a lot.

Yesterday, designer-couturier-jewellery maker, Sabyasachi Mukherjee opened his new store in Delhi. Spread across 26,000 square feet, is his largest yet in India. It has approximately 120 chandeliers, hundreds of artworks, antique carpets, textiles, mirrors and decorative objects. Over the years as Sabyasachi designed and redesigned his stores, adding spaces and retail categories, his visual language, obsession with oldness and his ability to turn nostalgia into desire became the stuff of writing.

It is hard to write a piece if you can’t breathe between the description of the objects that are the designer’s subjects. The tiger on the prowl in these rooms is not only the wild cat of Bengal that Sabyasachi is so intensely fond of but the problem of making sense of “more”. 

But what struck me for the first time was a sense of control in the curation of these museum-like stores. Look closely and nothing is chaotic. They are crowded with objects, but they are not confused. Each corridor leads the eye to somewhere else. Every room reveals another. There is clear choreography.

I had only one question for Sabyasachi. “How do you respond to a space that has nothing on it, is blank, without any colour, decoration or ornamentation? How does emptiness make you feel?”

Before blinking or breathing, he said “You are talking about my bedroom in my home in Kolkata.” It’s is bare. There is nothing on the walls. Nothing anywhere in it. “All this is my armour, my mask, my makeup, my theatre. This is not me. I am a minimalist at heart; a maximalist as a creator.”

Which is why, after walking through 26,000 square feet of Sabyasachi, I keep thinking about his room in Kolkata that he described to me with nothing on the walls.

What does rap have to do with handloom? Quite a bit, says Sanjay Garg, founder-designer of Raw Mango. The brand dropped a track this morning on Instagram in which tennis-player-turned-rapper Adil Kalyanpur belts out words like jamdani, ikat and brocade—and what nobody ever told “you” about why handlooms matter. The “you”, one hopes, is the young.
Kalyanpur, aka A-KAL, is Gen Z. More enjoyably, Garg says, he knew almost nothing about handlooms before the Raw Mango team approached him. In the rap, weaving vocabulary gets rhyme, rhythm and swagger.
The song, written by Garg and his team, is “osm”, as the young like to say. What it implies may not be as breezy. The foot tapping number leads to three subjects that Garg believes matter at the moment: jobs, identity and climate.
On the phone yesterday, the ever-passionate, breathlessly persuasive Garg described the rap as another addition to what Raw Mango has been stacking up around National Handloom Day over the years. Books, songs, stars and actors wearing Raw Mango—each year, he looks for another way in. Handloom Day, he insists, cannot only be about wearables or fashion. Nor is Garg interested in purist pursuits. He would rather “argue, disrupt, disagree” than service a familiar formula.
That is where the rap becomes more than a clever Handloom Day social media post. 
For years, India’s handloom conversations—including many we find today—have circled around three exhortations: wear it, buy it, praise the artisan. Handloom is positioned as ethical duty. All remain important, of course. But handloom cannot survive on worthiness alone. It must expand into other territories to become a loom of ideas, not just cloth.
Handloom is circular. Yet, given the chance, it can also soar or sing.
Garg does want us to know, though, that the rap was conceptualised and shot before the student protests taught us so vividly how to remain circular and fly.

British designer John Galliano’s return to mainstream fashion has unfolded in carefully calibrated acts: a 2013 residency at Oscar de la Renta, his appointment at Maison Margiela in 2014 and the Spring 2024 Artisanal show that became a viral sensation and reaffirmed his formidable talents as a couturier. Kevin Macdonald’s documentary High & Low—John Galliano followed, and in March came a two-year partnership with Zara to “re-author” its archives.
Now, comes the ultimate benediction: John Galliano: Horizons, the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition. Galliano will become the third living designer, after Yves Saint Laurent and Rei
Kawakubo, to be conferred this honour. A solo Met exhibition places a designer in fashion history; the gala turns it into global spectacle. And while Galliano is a compelling subject, he’s a treacherous one. In 2011, he
was dismissed from Dior and his eponymous label after uttering antisemitic and racist remarks and was later convicted by a French court. The Met says it will
confront this problematic history in an opening section ‘Bearings’. Curator Andrew Bolton has rejected a simple fall-and-redemption narrative, focusing instead on the tension between creative achievement and accountability. While Galliano’s romantic vagabonds, bias-cut heroines and theatrical Dior fantasies offer great dress-code material, will the evening devolve into an
absolving tribute? Or will ’Bearings’ serve as a neutral disclaimer to an exhibit devoted to a “disgraced” genius?
Met Gala’s lead chairperson Anna Wintour has been a long-time supporter of Galliano, but Bolton claims a more scholarly engagement, spanning years of writing and exhibitions. Reports say the duo and Galliano have met Jewish leaders and the Anti-Defamation League has acknowledged his apology and atonement. That context matters. Galliano’s contribution to fashion is too significant to erase, but his former misdemeanour can’t be reduced to a footnote in a triumphant career narrative. Can the Met Gala’s machinery of spectacle hold accountability without turning it into another theme, or is redemption already written on the horizon?

caption:
We, the people of India, are now highly literate in the language of public relations. We know what a statement sounds like when every potentially “troublesome” noun has been removed from it. We recognise that words like “healing”, “unity”, “our youth”, “coming together” and “difficult times” tell us what the person issuing them actually thinks. Nothing much.

Back in the day, we loved stars enough to write letters in blood, fast and pray for them, queue outside their homes for a glimpse or a touch. We bought movie tickets, copied haircuts and clothes, and bought products because famous faces told us to.

In return, celebrities gave us glamour, fantasy and that mysterious substance called stardom.
Social media dismantled much of that arrangement. Celebrity became content.
Now, the student protests of 2026 have exposed the consequence of that shift. Audiences no longer want only access to celebrities. They want to know what they stand for.

After all, every Instagram follower is an economic asset. Every fan is a potential cinema ticket, streaming view, endorsement consumer or amplifier. Celebrities ask audiences to care about their films, fashion, fitness, beauty brands, holidays, causes and lives.

It becomes increasingly difficult to tell those same audiences that public or political life is none of their business when something genuinely consequential occurs.
Young fans are asking a brutally simple question: If you want our attention when you are selling something, where are you when we need yours?

The Indian star has not fallen. Glamour is not going anywhere, and neither is fandom. But celebrity exceptionalism may finally be weakening.
The chasm between actors Naseeruddin Shah and Kangana Ranaut—the latter also a politician—in their apparent socio-political convictions and articulation is so wide that it is unlikely to ever close. India will clap for Virat Kohli when he scores runs for the country. But in our heart of hearts, we also know Kohli is unlikely to wear his heart on his sleeve when it comes to the right to protest.
